clocks.duty: Report cyber incidents to the CBN
clocks.applies_to: Banks and payment service banks under the CBN 2024 risk-based cybersecurity framework (S5)
clocks.requirement: Incident record with a countdown from detection and an export for the CBN

clocks.duty: Report a cyber threat or incident to the national or sectoral CERT (ngCERT, NigFinCERT)
clocks.applies_to: Organizations under the Cybercrimes Act as amended in 2024 (S5)

clocks.duty: Notify the data protection regulator of a personal-data breach likely to risk people's rights; notify affected people immediately if risk is high
clocks.applies_to: Data controllers under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (S6)
clocks.requirement: Breach workflow listing what was exposed, who is affected and what was done

clocks.duty: Screen an alert within 72 hours; file the suspicious transaction report within 24 hours after suspicion is confirmed (S9). Older summaries of the Act say 24 hours from the transaction
clocks.requirement: Two case timers: 72 hours from alert creation, 24 hours from confirmed suspicion; keep both configurable (see section 9)

clocks.duty: Report international transfers of US$10,000 or more
Maximum stop order by the NFIU or EFCC
clocks.applies_to: Any account or transaction in scope (S4)
clocks.requirement: Account hold with an automatic expiry and audit entry

clocks.duty: Investigation window for a suspect BVN before a transfer completes

gaps.title: CBN circulars not read directly
gaps.detail: The CBN site returned access errors, so REG-01 to REG-06 (instant payment guidelines of 12 March 2026), REG-08 and REG-09 (cash policy), and GOV-01 to GOV-08 (baseline standards of 10 March 2026) rest on law-firm and press summaries. Confirm amounts, scope and effective dates in the originals.

gaps.title: KYC tier limits conflict, so none are hard-coded
gaps.detail: The 2013 and 2016 circulars give tier 1 as a ₦50,000 single deposit and ₦300,000 balance; a 2017 mobile-money circular gives daily limits of ₦50,000, ₦200,000 and ₦5,000,000; one 2026 guide gives ₦30,000 and ₦500,000 for tiers 1 and 2. Keep tier limits as per-institution configuration, and use the current CBN circular for each customer.

gaps.title: Cash ceiling versus reporting threshold
gaps.detail: The ₦5m and ₦10m figures in the 2022 Act are ceilings on cash payments. The NFIU's goAML upgrade (S10) puts the currency transaction report threshold at the same ₦5m and ₦10m for domestic cash (REG-17), but the Act itself does not say so, so keep both values configurable.

gaps.title: Sanctions freeze timing
gaps.detail: Reports say freezes are "immediate" under the 2022 terrorism act but give no hour count; confirm the legal timeline.

gaps.title: Applicability
gaps.detail: Several controls bind banks, payment service providers or specific license types. Capture each tenant's license type so the right pack turns on.

gaps.title: Suspicious-report timing differs by source
gaps.detail: The NFIU guidelines (S9) say 72 hours to screen and 24 hours to file after suspicion is confirmed; the 2022 Act summaries (S4) say 24 hours from the transaction; SEC and Templars material for virtual-asset providers (S12) mentions 48 hours. REG-14 follows the NFIU; confirm with counsel.

gaps.title: Person of Interest count
gaps.detail: One report says 3,417 entries and another 13,417 (REG-13 uses the latter). The count does not change the rule, but check it against the portal.

gaps.title: Retention
gaps.detail: The Act says five years; some summaries say seven for certain records. GOV-08 uses five as the minimum and should be configurable upward.

gaps.title: Items that could not be confirmed
gaps.detail: The official SEC virtual-asset threshold (CRY-04 stays a tenant setting), any NCC rule on activity after a SIM swap (SIM-01 to SIM-03 are my design from the SIM replacement and NIN-linking rules, S11), the NFIU's Ponzi-scheme advisory (PON-01 is a typology rule, not a quoted threshold), the full FCCPC digital-lending text (S13 is thin), and whether the 2017 BVN watchlist circular (S14) is still the current version.

gaps.title: Rule logic is the library author's design
gaps.detail: Section 7B expresses each rule in notation I chose, using thresholds from sections 2 to 6. It is not a regulator format, and it has not been backtested on Nigerian data.

glossary.definition: An 11-digit number that identifies one person across every Nigerian bank, linked to their fingerprints and photo.
The number the National Identity Management Commission gives each registered person in Nigeria.
The checks an institution makes to confirm who a customer is before and while serving them.
The same checks for a company: who owns it, who runs it and what it does.
Someone who holds or held an important public role, or their close family or associates. They need extra checks because their position can be misused.
Deeper checks for higher-risk customers, such as where their money and wealth come from, and approval by a senior manager.
A report to the NFIU about activity that may be linked to crime. Its existence must not be revealed to the customer.
A report like an STR that covers suspicious behaviour rather than one transaction.
A report to the NFIU of a large domestic cash deposit, withdrawal or payment.
A report to the NFIU of a large international transfer.
The national agency that receives and analyses STRs, CTRs and other reports.
The body that keeps Nigeria's sanctions list and receives reports of matches.
The regulator of banks and payment providers in Nigeria.
The company that runs Nigeria's interbank payments, the BVN system and the Person of Interest portal.
The regulator of telecoms, including SIM replacement and linking phone numbers to NINs.
The regulator of investments, which since 2025 includes virtual assets such as crypto.

glossary.expansion: Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
glossary.definition: The consumer-protection regulator that registers and supervises digital lenders.
The online system the NFIU uses to receive reports from institutions.
Nigeria's main law against money laundering. It sets cash limits, reporting duties and record keeping.
Nigeria's law on handling personal data, including telling the regulator about breaches.
How often something happens in a short time, such as five transfers in ten minutes.
Splitting money into several smaller amounts to stay under a limit or a reporting threshold.
An account used to receive and pass on stolen or criminal money, often owned by someone recruited or deceived.
Many different people paying into one account in a short time.
One account paying out to many different people in a short time, often right after receiving money.
Linking a customer's banking app to one phone, so a new phone must be verified before it can be used.
